metadata.narrative: I’m on the purchasing committee for a community arts nonprofit, and we’re about to order a few thousand branded cotton T-shirts and hoodies. Vendors are pitching sustainable, ethical, organic, B Corp, WRAP, and traceable options, but the cheaper bids are hard to ignore. What should we actually ask suppliers before choosing, and how should we weigh price, worker pay, factory safety, forced-labor risk, certifications, and greenwashing? I’d like a practical due-diligence checklist, red flags, and a recommendation for what tradeoffs are reasonable if we have a limited budget but don’t want our merch to contradict our values.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A nonprofit ordering several thousand branded T-shirts and hoodies should treat supplier selection as a structured risk assessment, not just a price comparison, because demanding a low price and tight turnaround is itself a documented driver of low wages and excessive overtime in garment factories.

Ask each bidder to name the exact factory that will produce the order, disclose any subcontracting, and explain how it verifies subcontractors meet the same standards, since undisclosed subcontracting has let orders from major retailers end up in unauthorized sweatshops.
Ask what upfront payment percentage the vendor requires, since researchers note that net-30 terms can leave workers unpaid if a factory's cash flow collapses.

Ask what workers actually earn relative to the local living wage, not just the legal minimum, because industry estimates suggest fewer than one in ten garment workers producing for major brands earn a living wage, and most buyer contracts only require minimum-wage compliance.
Ask whether the factory allows an independent trade union, and try to corroborate compliance claims through a labor rights NGO or union contact rather than accepting the vendor's word alone.

Ask which specific standard applies—WRAP, SA8000, amfori BSCI, SMETA, or Fair Trade USA—and understand that BSCI, SMETA, and the Ethical Trading Initiative's Base Code are auditing frameworks, not pass/fail certifications, so registration alone does not guarantee good conditions.

A useful checklist is the five-step social compliance audit: opening meeting, health-and-safety walkthrough, payroll/attendance review, private worker interviews, and a closing meeting with a signed corrective action plan; ask vendors whether this occurred and whether the plan was completed.

Automatic audit-failure red flags to ask about include child labor, forced-labor indicators such as confiscated ID documents, serious safety hazards, physical abuse, and bribery of auditors, with China, India, Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Myanmar flagged as highest-risk sourcing countries.

Ask whether factories are covered by a legally binding safety agreement rather than only a voluntary code, because the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse that killed 1,134 workers, plus the Tazreen and Ali Enterprises fires, occurred at factories whose buyers had only voluntary commitments—prompting the legally binding Bangladesh Accord, a stronger model than internal brand audits alone.

On forced labor, ask vendors to state in writing whether any cotton or yarn originated from Xinjiang, China, which produces roughly 20 percent of the world's cotton, with about 16 percent of cotton apparel on U.S. shelves testing positive for Xinjiang-linked fiber; under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act such imports are presumed forced-labor-tainted unless proven otherwise.

Treat such answers skeptically, because a 2021 Sheffield Hallam University investigation traced 53 intermediary suppliers across ten countries funneling Xinjiang-linked yarn to 103 well-known global brands with no disclosure to buyers, showing self-reported sourcing claims are often unreliable.

Also ask about cotton origin beyond China, since forced labor has separately been documented in Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan harvests, and fair-trade certifiers still cannot fully verify farm-to-factory chains once cotton is blended in spinning mills.

When vendors cite organic, Fair Trade, WRAP, or B Corp status, ask for the certificate number, issuing body, and exact scope certified, since certifications often cover only one link of the chain—a "Fair Trade Certified" garment may verify only the sewing factory while leaving farming and dyeing unverified.

The Fair Trade USA apparel premium is a useful signal: factories receive roughly 10 percent of order value if workers earn only minimum wage, sliding to about 1 percent if workers already earn a living wage, with workers voting on how it is spent.

Do not treat WRAP certification as a wage or safety guarantee, because several WRAP-certified factories have been found with unpaid wages, child labor, or harassment despite WRAP's stated zero-tolerance policy.

If a vendor touts B Corp status, remember certification relies substantially on self-reported data; BrewDog lost its B Corp status over workplace-culture complaints, and Nespresso was publicly challenged by fellow B Corps over low farmer wages, so B Corp is one signal among several, not a labor guarantee.
B Corp only requires scoring 80 of 200 points across five weighted categories, so a strong environmental score can mask a mediocre worker score.

To spot greenwashing, watch for vague buzzwords like "eco-friendly" without supporting data, a small showcased "conscious" capsule beside mass uncertified production, and claims that are really just legal minimum requirements dressed up as initiatives.
Take this seriously: a Changing Markets Foundation study found roughly 60 percent of sustainability claims by major British and European fashion brands were unsubstantiated or misleading.

On price, use market data to sanity-check bids: a basic t-shirt fell in real terms from about £8.50 in 1970 to roughly £1.36–£1.50 by 2010–2013 as production shifted to lower-wage countries, while a UK brand sourcing from a Fair Wear Foundation living-wage factory prices its base tee near £36, showing the real cost spread between cheapest and verifiably ethical options.
Given a limited budget, treat forced-labor exposure and physical safety as non-negotiable floors, since these carry both moral and, increasingly, legal exposure under laws like the UFLPA.

Concretely, require every finalist to disclose factory name and location, confirm in writing no Xinjiang, Uzbek, or Turkmenistan cotton is used, and show a recent third-party audit with no unresolved critical findings, before comparing price at all.

Among bidders clearing that floor, accepting a mid-tier bundle—WRAP or BSCI plus a stated living-wage commitment—over full Fair Trade or GOTS certification is reasonable if budget cannot stretch to both, since the wage and safety floor matters more here than organic fiber content.

Where a modest premium is affordable, spend it on a documented living-wage commitment or Fair Trade-style premium rather than marketing-forward labels, since wage improvements reach workers directly while capsule collections are a recognized greenwashing pattern.

Finally, put these commitments into the purchase contract itself, since traditional contracts shift compliance risk onto suppliers and let buyers exit without remediation when problems surface, whereas contracts locking in fair pricing, realistic lead times, and remediation-first exit clauses produce better outcomes for workers.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

output.text:
A community arts nonprofit buying several thousand branded T-shirts and hoodies should treat supplier selection as a structured risk assessment rather than a simple price comparison, because demanding a low price and tight turnaround time is itself a documented driver of low wages and excessive overtime in garment factories.
[shard_03785_74326]

Before choosing a vendor, ask each bidder to name the exact factory or factories that will produce the order, disclose whether any portion of the work will be subcontracted, and explain how they verify that subcontractors follow the same standards, since undisclosed subcontracting has allowed orders from major retailers to end up in unauthorized sweatshops without the buyer's knowledge.
[shard_04405_8649]

Ask what percentage upfront payment the vendor requires and whether that structure has ever caused a factory to fail to pay workers, since researchers who work with garment factories note that net-30 payment terms can leave workers unpaid if a factory's cash flow collapses.
[shard_04405_8649]

Ask suppliers directly what wage workers actually earn relative to the local living wage, not just the legal minimum, because industry estimates suggest fewer than one in ten garment workers producing for major brands earn a living wage, and most buyer contracts only commit suppliers to local minimum-wage compliance.
[shard_02691_52949]

Ask whether the factory allows an independent trade union or worker representation, and try to have any social-compliance claims corroborated by a labor rights NGO or union contact rather than accepted solely from the vendor, since suppliers may tell buyers what they think buyers want to hear.
[shard_03785_74326]

On certifications, ask which specific standard applies—WRAP, SA8000, amfori BSCI, SMETA, or Fair Trade USA—and understand that BSCI, SMETA, and the Ethical Trading Initiative's Base Code are compliance and auditing frameworks rather than pass/fail certifications, so a supplier's registration in these systems does not by itself guarantee good conditions.
[shard_01041_27624]

A useful practical checklist is the five-step social compliance audit used by third-party auditors: an opening meeting, a health-and-safety walkthrough, a review of payroll and attendance documentation, private worker interviews, and a closing meeting with a signed corrective action plan, and buyers should ask vendors whether their factories have undergone this kind of audit and whether the resulting corrective action plan was completed.
[shard_05691_84230]

Automatic audit-failure red flags worth asking about explicitly include child labor, forced labor indicators such as confiscated ID documents or restricted freedom to quit, serious safety hazards, physical abuse, and bribery of auditors, and note that China, India, Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Myanmar are flagged as the highest-risk sourcing countries for these violations.
[shard_05691_84230]

On factory safety specifically, ask whether the supplier's factories are covered by a legally binding safety agreement rather than only a voluntary code of conduct, because the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse that killed 1,134 workers, the Tazreen fire, and the Ali Enterprises fire all occurred at factories whose buyers had only voluntary safety commitments, which is why the legally binding Bangladesh Accord was created and is considered a stronger model than internal brand audits alone.
[shard_04729_78332]

On forced labor, ask vendors to state in writing whether any cotton, yarn, or fabric in the order originated from Xinjiang, China, given that the region produces roughly 20 percent of the world's cotton and about 16 percent of cotton apparel on U.S. store shelves has been found to contain Xinjiang-linked fiber, and that under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act such imports are presumed to involve forced labor unless the importer proves otherwise.
[shard_06365_32183]

Treat this question skeptically rather than as a checkbox, because a 2021 Sheffield Hallam University investigation traced 53 intermediary suppliers across ten countries funneling Xinjiang-linked yarn to 103 well-known global brands with no disclosure to the buyer, showing that self-reported sourcing claims are often unreliable.
[shard_05111_31005]

Also ask about cotton origin beyond China, since forced labor has separately been documented in Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan cotton harvests, and note that fair-trade cotton certification bodies still cannot fully verify farm-to-factory chains once cotton is blended in spinning mills.
[shard_04717_81462]

When vendors cite organic, Fair Trade, WRAP, or B Corp status, ask for the certificate number, issuing body, and scope of what was actually certified, because certifications commonly cover only one link of the chain—for example, a "Fair Trade Certified" garment may only guarantee the sewing factory while leaving cotton farming and dyeing unverified.
[shard_04717_81462]

Understand the Fair Trade USA apparel premium mechanism as a useful signal: factories receive a social premium equal to roughly 10 percent of the order's freight-on-board value if workers are paid only minimum wage, sliding down to about 1 percent if workers already earn a living wage, and workers themselves vote on how the premium is spent.
[shard_00040_1501]

Do not treat WRAP certification as a wage or safety guarantee by itself, because several WRAP-certified factories have been found with unpaid wages, child labor, or worker harassment despite WRAP's stated zero-tolerance policy.
[shard_03543_62552]

If a vendor touts B Corp status, remember certification relies substantially on self-reported data, and note real cases such as BrewDog losing its B Corp status over workplace culture complaints and Nespresso being publicly challenged by fellow B Corps over low farmer wages, so B Corp status is one governance signal among several rather than a labor-conditions guarantee.
[shard_01142_80159]

Also note B Corp only requires scoring 80 out of 200 points across five weighted categories including environment, workers, community, governance, and customers, so a strong environmental score can mask a mediocre worker score.
[shard_00170_25886]

To spot greenwashing in a pitch, watch for vague, unsubstantiated buzzwords like "eco-friendly" or "sustainable range" without supporting data, a small showcased "conscious" capsule collection sitting alongside mass, uncertified production, and claims framed as innovations that are actually just legal minimum requirements.
[shard_01461_46711] [shard_03638_35511]

Take this risk seriously rather than as a minor marketing quirk, since a Changing Markets Foundation study found roughly 60 percent of sustainability claims made by major British and European fashion brands were unsubstantiated or misleading.
[shard_00731_45820]

On price, use market data to sanity-check bids rather than negotiating blind: a basic mass-market t-shirt fell in real terms from about £8.50 in 1970 to roughly £1.36–£1.50 by 2010–2013 largely because manufacturers shifted production to lower-wage countries, while a small UK brand sourcing from a Fair Wear Foundation-certified, living-wage factory prices its base tee at about £36, illustrating the real cost spread between the cheapest and most verifiably ethical options.
[shard_02081_59999]

Given a limited nonprofit budget, the most defensible tradeoff is to treat forced-labor exposure and physical safety as non-negotiable floors rather than negotiable line items, since these carry both moral and, increasingly, legal exposure under laws like the UFLPA.
[shard_06365_32183]

Concretely, require every finalist bidder to disclose factory name and location, confirm in writing that no Xinjiang, Uzbek, or Turkmenistan cotton is used, and show a recent third-party social-compliance audit report with no unresolved critical findings, before price is even compared.
[shard_05691_84230] [shard_04717_81462]

Among bidders that clear that floor, it is reasonable to accept a mid-tier certification bundle—such as WRAP or BSCI plus a stated living-wage commitment—over full Fair Trade or GOTS organic certification if the budget cannot stretch to both, since the wage and safety floor matters more for the specific harms this committee is trying to avoid than organic fiber content does.
[shard_01041_27624] [shard_00040_1501]

Where budget allows only a modest premium, prioritize spending it on the Fair Trade-style wage premium or a documented living-wage commitment rather than on marketing-forward labels like a small "eco capsule" line, since wage improvements reach workers directly while capsule collections are a recognized greenwashing pattern.
[shard_00040_1501] [shard_01461_46711]

Finally, put these commitments into the purchase contract itself rather than trusting verbal assurances, since responsible-contracting research shows that traditional contracts shift all compliance risk onto suppliers and let buyers exit without remediation when problems surface, whereas contracts that lock in fair pricing, realistic lead times, and a remediation-first exit clause produce better outcomes for workers.
[shard_02691_52949]

On price, use market data to sanity-check bids: a basic t-shirt fell in real terms from about £8.50 in 1970 to roughly £1.36–£1.50 by 2010–2013 as production shifted to lower-wage countries, while a UK brand sourcing from a Fair Wear Foundation living-wage factory prices its base tee near £36, showing the real cost spread between cheapest and verifiably ethical options.
Given a limited budget, treat forced-labor exposure and physical safety as non-negotiable floors, since these carry both moral and, increasingly, legal exposure under laws like the UFLPA.

Concretely, require every finalist to disclose factory name and location, confirm in writing no Xinjiang, Uzbek, or Turkmenistan cotton is used, and show a recent third-party audit with no unresolved critical findings, before comparing price at all.

Among bidders clearing that floor, accepting a mid-tier bundle—WRAP or BSCI plus a stated living-wage commitment—over full Fair Trade or GOTS certification is reasonable if budget cannot stretch to both, since the wage and safety floor matters more here than organic fiber content.

Where a modest premium is affordable, spend it on a documented living-wage commitment or Fair Trade-style premium rather than marketing-forward labels, since wage improvements reach workers directly while capsule collections are a recognized greenwashing pattern.

Finally, put these commitments into the purchase contract itself, since traditional contracts shift compliance risk onto suppliers and let buyers exit without remediation when problems surface, whereas contracts locking in fair pricing, realistic lead times, and remediation-first exit clauses produce better outcomes for workers.
